analogy.p: Imagine a layer of big, evenly sized **beach balls** (the positive ions) sitting in a pool of **tiny glitter** (the delocalised electrons). The glitter flows around everything and clings to all the balls, holding them together. If you push, the layers of balls roll over each other but stay stuck in the glitter, so the whole thing changes shape without falling apart: this is a **pure metal being bent**. Now mix in a few **oversized or undersized balls** (the alloy): the layers jam on the odd-sized balls and are much harder to push past each other, like an alloy. The analogy breaks down because real ions are held by electrostatic attraction, not by sticking, and the glitter (electrons) is what carries electric charge and heat when it flows.
analogy.t: A crowd of people in a ball pit

bullets: Know that **metals have giant structures** held together by **strong metallic bonding**.
Explain **high melting and boiling points** using the strong electrostatic attraction that must be overcome.
Explain **electrical conductivity** and **thermal conductivity** using **delocalised electrons**.
Explain why metals can be **bent and shaped** (layers of atoms slide over each other).
Explain why **pure metals are soft** and why **alloys are harder** (different sized atoms distort the layers).
Know examples of alloys and their uses (for example **steel**, **brass**, **bronze** and **gold alloys measured in carats**).
Marks range from 1 mark for naming an alloy up to 4 to 6 mark questions linking bonding to properties.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8462 section 4.2.2 says that **metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding**, which means **most metals have high melting and boiling points**. In **pure metals the atoms are arranged in layers**, which allows metals to be **bent and shaped**. **Pure metals are too soft for many uses**, so they are mixed with other metals to make **alloys**, which are **harder**. You must also explain why metals are **good conductors of electricity** (delocalised electrons carry charge) and **good conductors of thermal energy** (energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons). Higher marks come from linking every property to the **structure and bonding**.

bullets: Metal atoms are at the **left and centre of the periodic table**, with **1 to 3 electrons** in the outer shell (and transition metals), which they **lose easily**.
The structure is a **regular arrangement of positive ions** in layers, surrounded by **delocalised electrons**.
**Metallic bonding** = **electrostatic forces of attraction** between **positive metal ions** and **shared (delocalised) electrons**.
The bonding is **non-directional**: the electrons attract the ions in every direction, so the ions can move relative to each other without breaking the bonding.
Do not draw or describe 'metal atoms' sharing pairs of electrons as in covalent bonding; in metals the electrons are shared with **all** the ions.
Compare: **ionic** compounds have positive and negative ions in a lattice; **metals** have positive ions in a sea of electrons; **covalent** substances share pairs of electrons between atoms.
Pure **metals are elements** (one type of atom); **alloys** are mixtures.
core.h: The structure and bonding of a metal
core.p: A metal is made of a **giant lattice of positive metal ions** arranged in regular **layers**. The atoms of a metal **lose their outer-shell electrons** to become positive ions, and these outer electrons are **not attached to any one ion**: they are **delocalised**, forming a 'sea' of electrons that moves freely through the whole structure. **Metallic bonding** is the **strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the shared delocalised electrons**. This attraction holds the whole structure together in all directions, which is why metals are strong and have high melting points.

bullets: The **strong electrostatic attraction** between **positive ions and delocalised electrons** must be **overcome** to melt the metal.
A **giant structure** means there are **very many** attractions acting at once, so a lot of **energy** is needed.
**Boiling points** are higher still, because the ions must be **completely separated** from each other.
**Typical values** (you do not need to learn them): iron melts at about **1540 °C**, copper at about **1085 °C**, aluminium at about **660 °C**.

**Exception to remember**: Group 1 metals (e.g. sodium, melting at about **98 °C**) have **relatively low** melting points because they have only **one delocalised electron per ion** and larger ions, so the attraction is weaker; **mercury** is a liquid at room temperature.

Extension: in general, a metal with ions of **higher charge** (more delocalised electrons per atom) and **smaller ions** has stronger bonding and a higher melting point (e.g. magnesium melts at a much higher temperature than sodium).
core.h: Why most metals have high melting and boiling points
core.p: To melt a metal you must give the particles enough energy to **overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction** between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons so that the ions can move freely past one another. Because the metallic bonding is **strong** and acts throughout the **giant structure**, a **lot of energy** is needed. This is why most metals are solids at room temperature with **high melting and boiling points**. A good exam answer names the force (electrostatic attraction), says what is overcome, and says that a lot of energy is required.

bullets: **Delocalised electrons** are **free to move** throughout the metal.
Because electrons are **negatively charged**, they move towards the **positive terminal**; they **carry charge** through the metal.
The **positive ions do not move** in a solid metal; they stay in the lattice.
Metals conduct as **solids** because the electrons can move; **ionic compounds** only conduct when **molten or dissolved**, because their ions are fixed in the solid.
Exam phrase: '**delocalised electrons** that are **free to move** and **carry charge**'.
Metals conduct in **both solid and liquid states**, because the delocalised electrons are present in both.
core.p: To conduct electricity a substance needs **charged particles that are free to move**. In a metal, the **delocalised electrons** are **free to move through the structure**, and when a voltage (potential difference) is applied they **drift towards the positive end**, so they **carry the electric charge** through the metal. The positive ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice. Metals conduct both as **solids and liquids** because the delocalised electrons are present in both states. Always write 'delocalised electrons **carry charge**' to get the mark.

bullets: **Delocalised electrons** gain energy when heated, so they **move faster**.
They **transfer the energy** to other electrons and ions in cooler parts of the metal.
This is the reason metals are used for **saucepans**, **radiators** and **heat sinks**.

Non-metals such as diamond and most covalent substances have **no delocalised electrons**, so they are poor conductors of thermal energy (graphite is an exception because of its delocalised electrons).
Link to physics: thermal conduction is covered in the Energy topic; metals are the best conductors.
Always give the particle that transfers the energy (the **delocalised electrons**) in the explanation.
core.p: Metals are also **good conductors of thermal energy** (heat). When one end of a metal is heated, the **delocalised electrons gain kinetic energy** and move faster. They then **transfer this energy** through the structure to the cooler parts of the metal. This is why metal pans heat up quickly and why metals feel cold to touch: they conduct thermal energy away from your hand. AQA states simply that **energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons**.

bullets: In pure metals the atoms are arranged in **layers** (a regular lattice).
A force makes the **layers slide over each other**; the **metal changes shape** but does not shatter.
The **delocalised electrons** continue to **bond** the ions together in the new arrangement, so the structure holds.
**Malleable** = can be hammered or bent into shape; **ductile** = can be drawn into wires (both are used for metals).
Contrast: **ionic compounds are brittle**; **giant covalent substances (diamond)** are hard because the layers cannot slide.
Link to uses: copper is drawn into **wires**; aluminium is rolled into **foil**; iron is shaped into **sheets and girders**.
core.h: Why metals can be bent and shaped (malleable)
core.p: The positive ions in a pure metal are arranged in **regular layers**. When a force is applied, the **layers of atoms can slide over each other** without the metal breaking, so the metal can be **bent, hammered or drawn into wires**. This works because **metallic bonding is non-directional**: the delocalised electrons still hold the ions together after the layers have moved to new positions. In contrast, an **ionic crystal is brittle** because shifting the layers brings ions of the **same charge** next to each other, and the repulsion splits the crystal.

bullets: In a **pure metal** all the atoms are the **same size**, so they sit in **neat, regular layers**.
Regular layers **slide over each other easily** when a force is applied, so the metal is **soft** and easily bent.
Examples of soft pure metals: **gold, copper, aluminium, iron**.
Soft pure metals are not suitable for **tools, buildings or machinery** that must keep their shape under load.
The solution is to make an **alloy** (see next sections).
Do not say metals are 'weak'; say they are **soft/malleable** in pure form.
core.h: Why pure metals are too soft for many uses
core.p: Although metals are strong, **pure metals are often too soft** for everyday uses because their **layers of identical atoms slide over each other easily**. Pure iron, for example, bends too easily to make bridges or cars, and pure gold, copper and aluminium are soft. To make a metal **harder and stronger**, it is mixed with other elements to form an **alloy**. The key phrase: **pure metals are too soft for many uses and so are mixed with other metals to make alloys which are harder**.

bullets: Alloy = **mixture of a metal with other elements** (usually other metals; steel is iron with carbon).
The other atoms are **different sizes**, so they **disrupt (distort) the regular layers**.
It is **more difficult for the layers to slide** over each other.
Therefore the alloy is **harder** (and usually stronger) than the pure metal.
An alloy is a **mixture, not a compound**: the elements are not chemically bonded in fixed proportions, so the proportions can be varied to change the properties.
Alloys **still conduct electricity** because they contain delocalised electrons, and they still have **high melting points**.
Model sentence: 'The different-sized atoms distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, making the alloy harder than the pure metal.'
core.h: Alloys: what they are and why they are harder
core.p: An **alloy** is a **mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal** (most alloys are mixtures of metals, though steel contains carbon, a non-metal). In an alloy the added atoms are a **different size** from the atoms of the main metal. These different-sized atoms **distort the regular layers** of the structure, so the layers **cannot slide over each other as easily**. This makes the alloy **harder** than the pure metal. This is the standard explanation tested at GCSE and is worth 2 to 3 marks.

bullets: **Steel**: an alloy of **iron with carbon** (and sometimes other metals). **Low-carbon steel** is soft and easily shaped (car bodies); **high-carbon steel** is hard but brittle (tools, cutting edges); **stainless steel** (contains chromium and nickel) is **resistant to corrosion** (cutlery, sinks).
**Bronze**: an alloy of **copper and tin**; harder than copper; used for statues, medals, bells and ship fittings.
**Brass**: an alloy of **copper and zinc**; harder than copper; used for taps, door handles and musical instruments.
**Aluminium alloys**: have **low density** and are **strong**, so they are used to make **aircraft**.
**Gold alloys**: gold used for jewellery is an alloy with **silver, copper and zinc**, because pure gold is too soft; the proportion of gold is measured in **carats**.
Learn the **composition** (which elements) and a **use linked to a property** for each alloy above; that is what mark schemes reward.
Link: **pure iron** is rarely used; **cast iron** and **steels** are far more useful.
core.h: Examples of alloys and their uses
core.p: You should be able to name some common alloys, say what they contain and link their properties to their uses. Many of these examples also appear in the Using Resources topic, so learning them here helps in both. Always link the property that the alloy has (hardness, resistance to corrosion, low density) to the job it does.

bullets: **percentage of gold = (carat number ÷ 24) × 100**.
**24 carat** = **100%** gold (pure, but too soft for most jewellery).
To find the **mass of gold** in an object, multiply the object's mass by the percentage as a decimal: a 12 g ring of 18 carat gold contains 12 × 0.75 = **9 g** of gold.
**Why alloy gold?** It makes the jewellery **harder and more durable**, and also **cheaper**.
Give percentages to a sensible number of **significant figures** and show your working.
core.p: The **purity of gold** is measured in **carats**. **24 carat gold is 100% pure gold**, so a smaller carat number means more of the other metals. To convert a carat value into a percentage, divide the carat number by 24 and multiply by 100. These questions are good maths marks and are often combined with alloy explanations (why gold jewellery is not 24 carat).

bullets: **Metal**: high melting point (most), conducts as **solid and liquid**, **malleable and ductile**, **delocalised electrons**.
**Alloy**: similar to the metal but **harder**, due to **distorted layers**; still conducts.
**Ionic compound**: high melting point, **conducts only when molten or dissolved**, **brittle**.
**Simple molecular**: **low** melting point, **does not conduct**.
**Giant covalent**: **very high** melting point, **does not conduct** (except graphite), very hard.
To decide from data: if it **conducts when solid** it must have delocalised electrons (a metal or graphite); if it conducts only when **liquid**, it is **ionic**.
Explain using **particles and forces**: ions and electrons for metals, ions for ionic, atoms and covalent bonds for giant covalent.
core.h: Comparing metals, alloys and other structures
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare a metal with an ionic compound or covalent substance, or to explain which of several substances is a metal from data. Use **melting point, electrical conductivity (solid and liquid) and malleability** as clues. Metals **conduct as solids**, and are **malleable**, which sets them apart from ionic compounds (which only conduct when molten or dissolved and are brittle) and giant covalent substances (which are hard, do not conduct and do not bend).

bullets: **High melting point**: giant metallic structure; strong electrostatic attraction between ions and delocalised electrons must be overcome; a lot of energy.
**Conducts electricity**: delocalised electrons free to move; they carry the charge.
**Conducts thermal energy**: delocalised electrons transfer energy through the metal.
**Malleable**: layers of ions slide over each other; delocalised electrons keep ions bonded.
**Alloy harder**: different-sized atoms distort layers; layers cannot slide easily.
Avoid vague words such as 'strong bonds' on their own; say '**strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons**'.
core.h: Using bonding to explain properties: a method
core.p: The grade 9 skill is a **consistent, three-part explanation**: (1) name the **structure and bonding**, (2) say what is **overcome or what moves**, and (3) state the **effect on the property**. Using this pattern, you can answer any metal property question quickly and gain all the marks.

bullets: **Periodic table**: metals form **positive ions** by losing electrons; this is why they are on the left; Group 1 metals are soft with low melting points; **transition metals** have high melting points, are hard and strong, and are dense.
**Electrolysis and extraction**: metals that are less reactive than carbon are extracted by **reduction with carbon**; the metal is then often turned into alloys.
**Using resources**: **steel**, **brass**, **bronze**, **aluminium alloys** and **gold carats** are covered in more detail there.
**Physics**: electric current in a metal is a flow of **electrons (charge)**; resistance arises as they pass through the lattice of ions.
**Corrosion**: iron rusts but stainless steel resists corrosion because of chromium.
**Data questions**: use the properties table first (melting point, conductivity), then name the bonding.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam context
core.p: Metals and alloys link to **the periodic table** (metals lose electrons, Group 1 and transition metals), **the reactivity series and extraction** (obtaining metals from ores), **electrolysis** (metals as electrodes, copper purification), **corrosion and rusting** in the Using Resources topic, and **electricity** in Physics (resistance, current as flow of charge). Showing awareness of these links helps in extended answers.

exam: **1 mark (State/Name)**: e.g. 'alloy', 'delocalised electrons', 'steel is an alloy of iron and carbon'.
**Define metallic bonding (2 marks)**: strong electrostatic attraction (1) between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons (1).
**Explain high melting point (2 to 3 marks)**: giant structure/lattice; strong electrostatic forces between ions and delocalised electrons must be overcome; a lot of energy.
**Explain electrical conductivity (2 marks)**: delocalised electrons are free to move (1); they carry charge through the metal (1). Do not say ions move.
**Explain thermal conductivity (2 marks)**: delocalised electrons gain energy/move faster (1) and transfer the energy through the metal (1).
**Explain malleability (3 marks)**: layers of atoms/ions (1); layers slide over each other (1); delocalised electrons keep the ions bonded/structure holds (1).
**Explain why alloys are harder (2 to 3 marks)**: different-sized atoms (1); distort the layers (1); layers cannot slide over each other easily (1).
**Why not use pure metal? (2 marks)**: pure metals are too soft for many uses (1) because the layers slide easily (1).
**Carat calculations (2 to 3 marks)**: percentage = carat ÷ 24 × 100 (1 for method); show the substitution; give the answer with % or the mass in grams.
**Command words**: State = short fact; Describe = what happens; Explain = reason with because; Compare = both sides together using whereas; Suggest = apply knowledge to unfamiliar alloys or data.

**Data questions**: if an unknown solid conducts electricity, is malleable and has a high melting point, say 'metallic' and justify using delocalised electrons; if it conducts only when molten or dissolved, say 'ionic'.

mistakes.r: Metals conduct because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge; the positive ions stay in fixed positions.
mistakes.w: Metals conduct because the ions are free to move.

mistakes.r: Say: strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons must be overcome, which needs a lot of energy.
mistakes.w: Metals have strong bonds between atoms, so they have high melting points.

mistakes.r: The metallic bonding is strong; metals bend because the layers of ions slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep the ions bonded.
mistakes.w: Metals are malleable because they have weak bonds.

mistakes.r: Alloys are harder because different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
mistakes.w: Alloys are harder because the atoms are bonded more strongly.

mistakes.r: An alloy is a mixture (not a compound); the proportions can vary and the elements are not chemically combined in fixed ratios.
mistakes.w: An alloy is a compound of metals.

mistakes.r: In metals the outer electrons are delocalised (shared among all the ions); the metal atoms become positive ions.
mistakes.w: Metal atoms share pairs of electrons like covalent bonding.

mistakes.r: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because their ions are fixed; metals conduct because of delocalised electrons.
mistakes.w: Metals conduct electricity because they contain ions, like ionic compounds.

mistakes.r: Pure metals are often too soft for many uses because their identical atoms form regular layers that slide easily.
mistakes.w: Pure metals are hard because they have strong bonds.

mistakes.r: Most metals do, but Group 1 metals have relatively low melting points and mercury is a liquid at room temperature.
mistakes.w: All metals have high melting points.

summary: AQA 4.2.2: metals have giant structures of atoms (ions) with strong metallic bonding, giving most metals high melting and boiling points; in pure metals the atoms are in layers that can slide, so metals can be bent and shaped, and delocalised electrons make them good conductors of electricity and thermal energy. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed with other elements to make harder alloys. This matters because it is a classic structure-to-property explanation that is asked in almost every Chemistry paper.

terms.d: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between the positive metal ions and the shared delocalised electrons.
Outer-shell electrons of metal atoms that are not attached to one atom and are free to move through the whole structure.
A very large regular arrangement of particles in which the bonding extends throughout the whole lattice.
A positively charged particle formed when a metal atom loses its outer electrons.
A mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal; alloys are harder than pure metals.
Able to be hammered, bent or pressed into shape without breaking.
Able to be drawn out into a wire.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles, such as positive ions and negative electrons.
A substance that allows charge to flow through it, because it contains charged particles that are free to move.
An alloy of iron containing carbon (and sometimes other metals); low-carbon steel is soft and easily shaped, high-carbon steel is hard, stainless steel resists corrosion.
An alloy of copper and tin, harder than pure copper.
An alloy of copper and zinc, harder than pure copper.
A measure of the purity of gold; 24 carat is 100% pure gold.
The regular rows of ions in a pure metal that can slide over each other when a force is applied.
Breaks or shatters when a force is applied instead of bending (e.g. ionic compounds).
A regular repeating arrangement of particles in a solid.

worked.ans: Model answer: Copper has delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge, so it conducts electricity in wires. The delocalised electrons also transfer thermal energy through the metal, so it conducts heat in a saucepan. The layers of ions can slide over each other, so copper can be drawn into wires.
worked.q: Copper is used for electrical wires and for the base of saucepans. Explain why copper is suitable for both uses. (4 marks)
steps: Copper is a metal with a giant structure of positive copper ions surrounded by delocalised electrons.
Electrical wire: the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the metal (2 marks).
Saucepan base: the delocalised electrons transfer thermal energy through the metal (1 mark).
Wires also need to be drawn out: the layers of ions can slide over each other so copper is ductile/malleable (1 mark).

worked.ans: Model answer: Steel contains carbon atoms of a different size from iron atoms. These distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, making steel harder than pure iron.
worked.q: Pure iron is too soft to use in many buildings. Steel is much harder. Explain why steel is harder than pure iron. (3 marks)
steps: Steel is an alloy: iron mixed with a small amount of carbon (1).
The carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms, so they distort the regular layers of iron atoms (1).
This makes it more difficult for the layers to slide over each other, so steel is harder (1).

worked.ans: (a) 75% (b) 9 g (c) Pure gold is soft because its layers of identical atoms slide easily; mixing it with silver, copper or zinc distorts the layers, making the alloy harder and more suitable for jewellery.
worked.q: A ring is made from 18 carat gold and has a mass of 12 g. (a) Calculate the percentage of gold in 18 carat gold. (b) Calculate the mass of gold in the ring. (c) Explain why jewellery is not made from 24 carat gold. (5 marks)
steps: (a) 24 carat is 100% gold, so 18 carat = 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = 75% (1 mark method, 1 mark answer).
(b) Mass of gold = 75% of 12 g = 0.75 × 12 = 9 g (1 mark).
(c) Pure (24 carat) gold is too soft (1), because its layers of identical atoms slide over each other easily; alloying with other metals makes it harder (1).
